payload.claim: For VaR models tested with the Kupiec-POF test, the likelihood of a Type-II error (failing to reject a misspecified model) increases as the backtesting sample size falls, as the VaR model's confidence interval increases, and as the Kupiec-POF test's own confidence level increases.

source.locator: section: What we already know about backtesting and the Kupiec-POF test
source.title: Testing the test: How reliable are risk model backtesting results?

testability.notes: Simulation-validated relationship rather than a trading rule, but directly testable via Monte Carlo replication of the Kupiec-POF test.

payload.claim: Increasing the backtesting sample size or lowering the VaR confidence level makes the Kupiec-POF test's non-rejection area tighter and more symmetric, reducing the likelihood of a Type-II error.
payload.quote: As the backtesting sample size increases or the VaR confidence level declines the shape of the non-rejection area becomes “tighter” and more symmetric. This implies that if a user were to do either, the likelihood of experiencing a type II error would be lower.

source.locator: section: The distribution of the Kupiec-POF test statistic
source.title: Testing the test: How reliable are risk model backtesting results?

data_required: simulated P&L return series at varying sample sizes
Kupiec-POF test p-values and non-rejection regions

payload.claim: When the backtesting sample size is as small as 250 days or the VaR confidence level is as high as 99.5%, the Kupiec-POF test's non-rejection area is skewed and bounded to the left, so the test struggles to reject a risk model that produces zero breaches.
payload.quote: when the sample size is small (e.g. 250 days) or the VaR confidence level is high (e.g. 99.5%) the shape of the non-rejection area is skewed and bounded to the left. This indicates that the test will struggle to reject a risk model producing zero breaches even if the test has been designed to do so.

source.locator: section: The distribution of the Kupiec-POF test statistic
source.title: Testing the test: How reliable are risk model backtesting results?

data_required: simulated/historical P&L return series of 250 days
VaR model breach counts at 99.5% confidence

payload.claim: Under a Normal P&L distribution assumption, the Kupiec-POF test is less likely to reject (fail) a VaR model that over-estimates volatility than one that under-estimates volatility by the same amount, and this asymmetry worsens as the VaR/test confidence interval increases or the backtesting sample size is reduced.
payload.quote: A simple visual inspection of these charts supports our previous expectation that the probability of experiencing a type II error is asymmetric around the correctly specified volatility. In particular, our results suggest that the Kupiec-POF test is in fact less likely to fail a VaR model which over-estimates volatility when compared to one that under-estimates volatility. Interestingly, this phenomenon worsens as the VaR/test confidence interval increases or the sample size is reduced.

source.locator: section: Interesting results from our simulation-based analysis (Figure 2, Normal model)
source.title: Testing the test: How reliable are risk model backtesting results?

data_required: VaR models with volatility misspecified between 0.7 and 1.3 of true value
Kupiec-POF test rejection rates across sample sizes and confidence intervals

payload.claim: When P&L returns follow a Student-t distribution, the likelihood of a Type-II error in the Kupiec-POF test increases substantially as the distribution becomes more fat-tailed (lower degrees of freedom), and this effect, along with the asymmetry between over- and under-estimated volatility, is worsened by reducing the backtesting sample size or increasing the VaR/test confidence interval.
payload.quote: Interestingly, we can see that as the distribution of the P&L returns becomes more fat-tailed the likelihood of a type II error increases substantially. This is evidenced by analysing the difference between the blue and red lines above. The graphs also reinforce the phenomenon of asymmetry, as explained previously. Again, reducing the backtesting sample size or increasing the VaR/test confidence interval worsens both of these effects.

source.locator: section: Interesting results from our simulation-based analysis (Figure 3, Student-t model)
source.title: Testing the test: How reliable are risk model backtesting results?

data_required: simulated Student-t distributed P&L return series with 3 and 9 degrees of freedom
Kupiec-POF test rejection rates across sample sizes and confidence intervals

payload.claim: When P&L returns follow a standardised skewed Student-t distribution, the Kupiec-POF test's Type-II error effects are more pronounced when the distribution is both fat-tailed and negatively skewed compared to positively skewed.
payload.quote:
However, it’s also clear that these effects now become much more pronounced when the P&L distribution is more “fat-tailed”
and
negatively skewed (as the blue lines are always above their red counterparts).

source.locator: section: Interesting results from our simulation-based analysis (Figure 4, Skew-t model)
source.title: Testing the test: How reliable are risk model backtesting results?

data_required: simulated standardised skewed Student-t P&L return series with 3 degrees of freedom and 0.7/1.3 skew parameters

payload.claim: The simulation-based test of the Kupiec-POF test's reliability misspecifies a VaR model's volatility by up to 30% (standard deviation values ranging from 0.7 to 1.3 relative to the true value of 1) to study the test's rejection rate behavior.
payload.quote: In each case, the standard deviation or volatility of the “correct” model, which is set equal to one, is deliberately misspecified using a range of values between 0.7 and 1.3. Here, the model will over-estimate (under-estimate) volatility if its standard deviation is higher (lower) than one, by a maximum of 30%.

source.locator: section: Interesting results from our simulation-based analysis
source.title: Testing the test: How reliable are risk model backtesting results?

payload.claim: Standard neural operator (NO) architectures used to predict European call-price surfaces from market or model features can produce arbitrage-violating outputs that lead to negative PnL when used in downstream trading tasks.
payload.quote: However, standard NO architectures cannot guarantee static no-arbitrage when predicting European call-price surfaces from market or model features and, as we verify experimentally, can yield negative PnL in downstream trading tasks.

source.title: AFNO: Universal Certifiably-Arbitrage-Free Operator Learning Framework for European Call-Price Surfaces

market or model features used as NO inputs

payload.claim: For monthly Rule 605 order execution reports from market maker Virtu and broker-dealer SoHo covering January 2021 to March 2024, standard predictive methods (linear regression and LSTM) perform poorly at forecasting the probability laws of stock orders despite those probability laws being relatively stable over time.
payload.quote: The paper analyzes monthly reports of two companies: one market maker, Virtu, and one broker-dealer, SoHo, in the period between January 2021 and March 2024. The predictive power of standard methods for the probability laws of stock orders- linear regression and LSTM- is poor, despite their probability laws being relatively stable.

source.title: Making sense of rule 605

testability.notes: Claim is at the generality the abstract supports; no specific parameter or error metric given.

payload.claim: The month-to-month correlations within the Rule 605 datasets (from Virtu and SoHo, Jan 2021-Mar 2024) are highly stable and predictable, in contrast to the poor predictive performance of linear regression and LSTM on the underlying probability laws.
payload.quote: However, the month-to-month correlations are highly stable and predictable.

source.title: Making sense of rule 605

testability.notes: No specific correlation metric or threshold named; claim kept at abstract's generality.

payload.claim: The statistical distributions of sixteen datasets derived from the 26 stock-trading parameters that brokerages report under Rule 605 regulatory requirements can be characterized and studied.

payload.claim: Strategy (MSTR) stock will experience selling pressure around the Nov. 30, 2026 close as index-tracking funds rebalance following its removal from the MSCI USA Index.
payload.quote: MSCI will remove Strategy, the largest corporate bitcoin holder, from the MSCI USA Index as of the close of Nov. 30, the index provider said Wednesday, after a new screen classified the company as a non-operating issuer.

source.title: MSCI Removes Strategy (MSTR) From Its USA Index, Forcing Index Funds to Sell by Nov. 30

data_required: MSTR daily/intraday price and volume data around Nov 30 2026
testability.notes: Classic index-deletion price pressure hypothesis testable via event study.

payload.claim: Forced selling by MSCI-tracking funds following Strategy's index exclusion is estimated at roughly $2.8 billion in outflows from MSTR, potentially rising to about $8.8 billion more if other index providers follow, a magnitude testable against actual realized trading volume and price impact around the Nov. 30, 2026 effective date.
payload.quote: Funds that track an MSCI index have to hold what the index holds, so they will have to sell the deleted stocks by the Nov. 30 close. JPMorgan analysts estimated last November that an exclusion could drive about $2.8 billion of outflows from Strategy, and as much as $8.8 billion more if other index providers followed. That estimate was built on MSCI’s earlier digital-asset proposal, not the October screen, and MSCI itself has published no figure.

payload.claim: A company is deemed ineligible for MSCI Global Investable Market Indexes if its operating assets fall below 50% of total assets and it is flagged on four or more of five specified financial ratios, a rule that can be applied retroactively to identify which companies are at risk of future MSCI index deletion.
payload.quote: The index first checks whether a company’s operating assets equal at least 50% of total assets. Issuers that fail that core screen face five financial ratios, and a company flagged on four or more of them is ineligible for the MSCI Global Investable Market Indexes.

payload.claim: Under MSCI's buffer rule, an index constituent is only removed if it fails the non-operating-issuer ineligibility screen in each of its two most recent annual filing periods, while a non-constituent is barred from addition if it fails in either period, a rule structure that can be used to model turnover timing in MSCI indexes.
payload.quote: A company outside the indexes cannot be added if it fails the ineligibility screen in either of its two most recent annual filing periods, but a current constituent is removed only if it fails in each of them.

payload.claim: The Dallas Fed survey's Future General Business Activity Index correlates strongly with the stock market when shifted forward by a 3-month adjustment, making it a 3-month leading indicator for stock price changes.
payload.quote: The index of Future General Business Activity is nice because it correlates very strongly with the stock market. But more importantly, that correlation comes after applying a 3-month adjustment. In other words, that index gives us a 3-month leading indication for what stock price changes are going to look like.

source.title: Dallas Fed Survey Has a Pearl of an Index

data_required: Dallas Fed Texas Manufacturing Outlook Survey Future General Business Activity Index (unadjusted)

payload.claim: Important stock price tops tend to arise when the Future General Business Activity Index forms a divergent lower top relative to the stock market.
payload.quote: It is an interesting feature of this relationship that important price tops tend to arise when there is a divergent lower top in this Future General Business Activity Index. Right now there is no divergence.

source.title: Dallas Fed Survey Has a Pearl of an Index

data_required: Dallas Fed Texas Manufacturing Outlook Survey Future General Business Activity Index
testability.notes: Vague on exact divergence definition and timing.

payload.claim: When the Future General Business Activity Index shows no divergence from rising stock prices, this indicates no major stock market top is likely within the next 3 months and prices should be expected to go higher.
payload.quote: A non-divergence can be even better, because it says there is no indication of a big important top coming, at least during the next 3 months. Some future divergence might develop, someday, but for now the message is that stock prices should be expected to go higher.

source.title: Dallas Fed Survey Has a Pearl of an Index

data_required: Dallas Fed Texas Manufacturing Outlook Survey Future General Business Activity Index

payload.claim: A dip to a negative reading in the Future General Business Activity Index resets the clock for measuring divergence, such that a valid divergence signal requires the index to remain above zero (no negative dip) between the comparison points.
payload.quote: This is because that dip to a negative reading in this index resets the clock for measuring any divergence. A proper divergence needs to appear between this index and prices without such a dip to a negative reading.

source.title: Dallas Fed Survey Has a Pearl of an Index

data_required: Dallas Fed Texas Manufacturing Outlook Survey Future General Business Activity Index

payload.claim: The German 10yr-3mo term spread inverted at 2022M12 and a plain vanilla spread probit regression implied a 70% probability of a German recession (as labelled by ECRI).
payload.quote: The 10yr-3mo German spread, hitherto a pretty good predictor, inverted at 2022M12. Hitherto a pretty good predictor of German recessions (as labelled by ECRI), the implied probability was 70%, using a plain vanilla spread regression.

source.title: What Did the German Term Spread Predict for 2024?

testability.notes: Testable via probit regression on term spread data.

payload.claim: A probit regression on the German 10yr-3mo term spread and short rate, using a 40% probability threshold, correctly predicts all ECRI-defined German recessions except the 2020 recession, but generates a false positive signal for 2024.
payload.quote: As shown in Figure 1, all recessions save the 2020 recession, are predicted using a 40% threshold. But a false positive is also recorded for 2024 using this same threshold.

source.locator: section discussing Chinn and Ferrara (2026) results
source.title: What Did the German Term Spread Predict for 2024?

payload.claim: Adding expected change in unemployment to the term spread probit regression increases pseudo-R2 from 0.19 to 0.29 relative to the basic spread specification over the same sample, but still produces a false positive recession signal for 2024 at a 40% threshold.
payload.quote: Including the expected change in unemployment yields results with slightly greater proportion of variation explained (0.29 relative to a basic specification estimated over the same sample period at 0.19). The recession predictions are much the same as the basic specification, however, with a false positive still registered for 2024, using the 40% threshold.

source.title: What Did the German Term Spread Predict for 2024?

payload.claim: Among German economic indicators, the peak dates for employment (2024Q4), real GDP (2022Q3), industrial production (February 2023), and term-spread-based recession probability (2024M12) show almost no coherence with each other.
payload.quote: Notice there is almost no coherence between the peak-to-trough periods. Peak employment is 2024Q4, peak GDP is 2022Q3, peak industrial production is February 2023, while peak recession probability is 2024M12.

source.title: What Did the German Term Spread Predict for 2024?

testability.notes: More descriptive/observational than a direct trading rule, but testable by comparing peak dates across series.

payload.claim: Across professional inflation forecasts, inflation swap markets, inflation option markets, and realized inflation, measured inflation uncertainty is flat for outcomes below the central bank's announced inflation target and rises linearly for outcomes above it, with a kink located at the announced target value.
payload.quote: A public that cannot verify the bank's intention prices each expected point of overshoot, so uncertainty about inflation is flat below the announced target and rises linearly above it: the observational-equivalence effect. Professional forecasts, swap and option markets and realized inflation all show this pattern, with the kink at the announced number.

source.title: Tolerable Inflation, Intolerable Uncertainty

testability.notes: Pattern claimed across four distinct data sources; testable as a piecewise relationship between distance-from-target and dispersion/implied volatility of each series.

payload.claim: In realized inflation data, inflation volatility rises with the level of inflation, and this level effect is mostly attributable to the energy component of inflation.
payload.quote: A second and larger effect produces the same shape: inflation is more volatile when it is high, and in realized inflation that level effect is mostly energy.

source.title: Tolerable Inflation, Intolerable Uncertainty

data_required: realized CPI/HICP inflation series with component breakdown
testability.notes: Testable by regressing realized inflation volatility on inflation level and decomposing by CPI component (energy vs. core).

source.title: Tolerable Inflation, Intolerable Uncertainty

data_required: French corporate loan-level interest rate data
testability.notes: Directly testable regression result with specific named dataset (French loan-level data) and quantified coefficient (89bps).

payload.claim: In an SDF-portfolio model where softmax-constrained weights are regularised by a ridge penalty that is minimised on the simplex at exactly 1/N, the model's default output is the equal-weighted portfolio, with any learned cross-sectional signal expressed only as a tilt away from 1/N.
payload.quote:
Long-only and fully invested hold exactly. Since an untrained network produces near-uniform scores, training starts at equal weight; combined with the ridge penalty, which on the simplex is minimised at exactly 1/
N
, the model’s default state is the equal-weighted portfolio and everything it learns is a tilt away from it.

payload.quote: The rank correlation of 0.53 between weights and realised returns shows the model found the signal: the ordering is largely right. And yet the weights span only 4.75 % to 5.23 % around an equal weight of 5.00 %, a mean absolute deviation of six basis points.

payload.claim: For SDF portfolios trained with a ridge-penalised Hansen-Jagannathan loss and softmax simplex weights, the maximum permitted deviation from the equal-weighted (1/N) portfolio is set primarily by the ridge coefficient λ and the simplex constraint rather than by representation quality, so apparent mild outperformance over 1/N in such models may be largely a mechanical artifact of regularisation rather than genuine signal.

As the worked example shows, how far the book may depart from equal weight is set by

N

payload.claim: A causal timestamp mask on the retrieval bank prevents direct retrieval of future information, but if the model's encoders, denoiser, and allocation head are trained once on the full sample rather than via walk-forward retraining with a bank built as of each evaluation date, every evaluation period will have been seen during training, constituting a leakage channel that masking alone does not close.
payload.quote: A correct mask prevents retrieval from the future. It does nothing about information entering through the parameters: if encoders, denoiser and head are trained once on the full sample, then every evaluation period was seen in training. Only walk-forward retraining with a bank built as of each date closes that channel, and it multiplies the computational cost.

payload.claim: For U.S. banks that drew only on the Fed's Discount Window during the March 2023 bank run, a stock-return-based 'beta' measuring investor sensitivity to uninsured deposit reliance and bank capital strength rose significantly 4-7 trading days after the bank's first DW borrowing, with sensitivity to capital elevated over the full 7-day post-borrowing window.
payload.quote: For banks that used only the DW, investors’ sensitivity to uninsured deposits and bank capital rose (i.e., the beta increased) significantly 4-7 days after borrowing. Indeed, sensitivity to bank capital was higher over the entire 7- day period after the first DW loan.

payload.claim: For U.S. banks that drew only on the Bank Term Funding Program during the March 2023 bank run, there was no statistically significant change in the stock-return-based beta measuring investor sensitivity to the bank's balance-sheet risks after the bank's first BTFP borrowing.
payload.quote: For banks that used only the BTFP, there was no significant change in investor risk perceptions. Thus, investors did not penalize banks for using the BTFP.

payload.claim: In the period from January 3 to May 5, 2023, the beta measuring bank stock investors' sensitivity to balance-sheet risk factors (uninsured deposits, unrealized securities losses, cash holdings, and CET1 capital) was statistically indistinguishable from zero before March 7, 2023, but became positive and increased sharply starting just before that date as the 2023 bank run began.
payload.quote: The chart below shows that beta was statistically zero (i.e., the confidence interval straddles zero) before the bank run, implying that stock investors were relatively unconcerned about bank risk. Just before the run started (on March 7), the beta becomes positive and increases sharply – that is, investors became highly sensitized during the run.

payload.claim: Among a sample of publicly traded banks, those making their first draw on the BTFP (34 banks) or DW (33 banks) between March 8 and March 31, 2023 can be compared against 207 non-borrowing banks using stock returns in the seven trading days before and after the first loan to detect differential changes in investor risk perception.
payload.quote: Between March 8 and March 31, 2023, 34 banks in our sample made a first draw on the BTFP and 33 on the DW; among these institutions, 10 used both facilities.
